seq.text: A rescue swimmer named Brendan Kiley reached a small, one-story house in the Houston area. Five people were waiting on the roof. Beside the house, the water was almost up to the top of a car.
A woman on the roof slid a big plastic bin toward him. He thought it was her luggage. The helicopter needed every seat for people, so he told her they could not take it.
She pushed it at him again.
His crew had flown in from Cape Cod, Massachusetts. Hurricane Harvey had come ashore in Texas and then stalled, dropping rain on Houston for days.
Catastrophic flooding was forecast days in advance. Why did so many people still end up trapped?
Five days earlier, Harvey had fallen apart over the Caribbean. On Wednesday, August twenty-third, it came back to life over the Gulf of Mexico, and grew fast.
On Friday morning, the National Hurricane Center warned of catastrophic, life-threatening flooding. By the afternoon it gave numbers: fifteen to thirty inches of rain, in places forty.

The same afternoon, forecasters put greater Houston under their highest flood risk, three days ahead. Their own review later called it unprecedented. What the forecast could not show was which streets would flood.

At Coast Guard Air Station Cape Cod, the pilot Simon Greene later recalled how fast it changed that Friday: their normal afternoon flights were cancelled, and they waited for the word to send a crew south.
In Houston, officials had a different decision to make. Several coastal counties ordered people out. For Houston and Harris County, there was no general evacuation order.
County Judge Ed Emmett explained why. When a storm surge comes in from the sea, you know who lives in its path. With rain, he said, you don't know which neighbourhoods are going to be affected.

And they remembered Hurricane Rita in 2005. As millions tried to leave the Houston area, dozens of people died during the evacuation, twenty-three of them in a single bus fire on the highway, before Rita came ashore.
At about ten on Friday night, Harvey came ashore near Rockport as a Category 4 hurricane. Then it stopped moving.
On Saturday night, the rain bands settled over Houston. One gauge recorded more than three inches in thirty minutes. At 9:27, the weather service issued its first flash flood emergency.
In parts of the county, about twenty-five inches fell in two days. Most of it came in nine to twelve hours, much of it overnight, while people slept.
South-east of the city, in Dickinson, the house of a Coast Guard chief, Matthew Dusek, flooded that weekend.

We had sewage come up through our showers and our bathtubs. So pretty much the night that it was happening it was up to our box springs, and we were pretty much walking around in sewage water and whatever else.
According to an Air National Guard report, when the water started filling his house, he took his boat and spent the day pulling his neighbours out.
By Sunday morning, Harris County's 911 system had taken fifty-six thousand calls in fifteen hours. The county judge asked for help.

Early on Sunday, a Houston police sergeant, Steve Perez, set out for work. According to the police chief, his wife had asked him not to go; he told her he had work to do. He drowned in his patrol car on a flooded road in north Houston.
That Sunday, Coast Guard aircraft from Cape Cod arrived over Houston. Kiley's helicopter crew came by way of Lafayette, Louisiana.

Most of their calls were just addresses from 911. Greene said they were told to follow the roads. Whichever pilot was not flying typed each address into Google Maps on a phone and called out the turns, like a driver.
It was his second day in Houston. Kiley had been lowered to that house, got onto the car, and climbed up to the five people on the roof. What worried him most was losing one of them off the edge.
He had told the woman to take out whatever she needed, something she could hold. She pushed the bin back at him. He remembers her words: 'No, that's my babies in there.'
He opened the lid. Inside, keeping dry, were a toddler and a newborn baby.
Kiley carried the bin down from the roof, helped the mother down after it, and put all three into the rescue basket for the hoist.
Afterwards, he said the bin had been a good call by their mother: inside it, the children were out of the rain and the wind, and they could not slide off the roof.

Rain was the other problem. When the heaviest bands came through, Greene said, the pilots could not see. They would set down in a ballpark or a car park, wait for the band to pass, and lift off again.
On the ground, Harris County's firefighters and police recorded more than sixty-one thousand rescues. Nobody counted the people saved by neighbours in their own boats.
Military police units drove into the floodwater in trucks. Sergeant Anthony Lara's first mission was in Dickinson.

When we first hit ground we did a mission with the Texas Search and Rescue team, and we went out to Dickinson. The water was probably, I'd say, maybe three feet deep. It got too deep to go in, but we were able to rescue some civilians that did come up to us with civilian boats that came up to our vehicles. We escorted them back, and then from there took them to shelters.
In League City, Specialist Kyle Wampler's unit worked with the local police.

We got to go out and perform a rescue on a elderly house, and you know, pulling this guy out. And he can barely walk, and just having to help him, even into our trucks and stuff like that. It just really stood out to me, because I know that if we weren't there to help 'em, that, you know, I don't know who else would or could have.
Almost everywhere in Houston, the water came from the rain and from overflowing bayous. But west of downtown, a different problem was building, behind two dams.

Addicks and Barker are earthen dams built in the 1940s to catch floodwater before it reaches the city. On August twenty-fifth, as Harvey approached, the Army Corps of Engineers closed their gates, as planned.
The basins filled. And inside them, on private land, whole neighbourhoods had been built. More than nine thousand homes and businesses there flooded, from water that was being held back.

Downstream, Buffalo Bayou was already running high from rain on the city. Around midnight on August twenty-eighth, with the pools still rising, the Corps began releasing water through the gates. Its reason was the safety of the dams: it had estimated that a dam failure would put six hundred thousand lives at risk.
According to the governor's commission, the releases flooded about four thousand homes along the bayou. On August thirtieth, both reservoirs reached their highest levels on record.

Years later, federal courts ruled that by flooding these homes to protect others, the government had taken private property and owed compensation. One court praised the Corps' professionalism, and found that, at the levels the water actually reached, the risk of a dam failure had been minimal.
Harvey finally drifted east. Its heaviest rain of all fell near Beaumont and Port Arthur: more than sixty inches at Nederland.
Near Beaumont, an Air Force Reserve crew lowered a pararescueman to a flooded house. He came back up with an elderly woman in the basket.
In Vidor, a pararescue team from the Alaska Air National Guard worked the streets by boat.

What we're doing here is providing boat teams in and out of these very flooded streets. Many times past the windows, we've seen cars completely submerged. These people need a way out. / Vidor's been fantastic. Everybody that we've come upon has helped us, either with boat trailers, because we've had a hard time accessing dry or wet land. They've helped us out with food, or just come up to us, shook our hands and thanked us. It's a pretty rewarding experience, seeing the best of America down here.
When the water went down in Dickinson, Matthew Dusek spoke to his insurance adjuster.
Just talked to the claims adjuster and it kinda sent me into a little spin, 'cause I don't have a house. I'm homeless. I don't know.
Harvey killed sixty-eight people directly, thirty-six of them in Harris County. In the county, about a hundred and fifty-four thousand houses flooded.
So why were so many people trapped, after a warning that came days ahead?
The forecast was right about the scale, and about the area. It could not name the streets. Then most of the rain fell in a single night, and the roads flooded before morning.

There was no general order to leave Houston. The officials' reasons were that nobody could say which neighbourhoods would flood, and that in Rita, the evacuation itself had killed people. That November, the county wrote that it would make the same decision again.

By Sunday morning, the way out for many people was a boat, a truck or a helicopter, and the 911 system was overwhelmed. In west Houston, water held back flooded thousands of homes, and water let through flooded thousands more.

Across Texas, first responders rescued more than a hundred and twenty-two thousand people. The Coast Guard rescued more than eleven thousand. In three days, Brendan Kiley's crew rescued a hundred and twelve.
